Stephen Sondheim was born in 1930 and died in 2021. He was a legendary American composer and lyricist, widely regarded as the most important and influential figure in late twentieth-century musical theater. Over six decades, he fundamentally revolutionized the American musical through his intricate, witty lyrics, sophisticated harmonic language, and willingness to tackle dark, unconventional subject matter.

His most famous work is Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street, which premiered in 1979. This operatic musical thriller tells the story of a vengeful barber who murders his customers in Victorian London, and whose corpses are then baked into meat pies by his partner Mrs. Lovett. In 1984, he created Sunday in the Park with George, a Pulitzer Prize-winning musical inspired by Georges Seurat's pointillist masterpiece A Sunday on La Grande Jatte. The show explores the obsessive nature of artistic creation. Another celebrated work, Into the Woods from 1987, intertwines and deconstructs Brothers Grimm fairy tales including Cinderella, Rapunzel, and Jack and the Beanstalk, exploring the complex moral consequences of happily ever after.

Company, which opened in 1970, was a pioneering concept musical with no linear plot. It centers on Bobby, a single thirty-five-year-old bachelor in New York, as he contemplates commitment through his interactions with his married friends. Before these triumphs, Sondheim collaborated on two landmark early Broadway musicals. West Side Story premiered in 1957 with music by Leonard Bernstein and lyrics by Sondheim. Then came Gypsy in 1959, with music by Jule Styne and lyrics by Sondheim.

Among his many individual songs, one of the most famous is Send in the Clowns, a melancholic ballad from his 1973 musical A Little Night Music. It became his most well-known individual song, covered by Frank Sinatra, Judy Collins, and many others.

Sondheim's work brought the musical theater tradition into close dialogue with modern classical harmony, and his collaboration with Leonard Bernstein on West Side Story demonstrated how his lyrics could match the dynamism of Bernstein's groundbreaking rhythms.
